questions.prompt: A React screen re-renders the entire order table on every keystroke in an unrelated search box. Most likely cause?
options: React is just slow with big tables.
A missing key prop on the table rows.
The component isn't wrapped in a context provider.
State that only one component needs was lifted too high, so the whole subtree re-renders.
questions.explanation: State lives at the lowest common ancestor that needs it — no higher. Hoisting the input's value into a parent makes every sibling re-render on every character. Missing keys are a real bug, but they cause wrong reconciliation, not extra renders.

questions.prompt: This hook was shipped last week. The API team noticed. Why?
options: It should use axios instead of fetch.
The .then chain needs a .catch.
No dependency array — it refetches after every render, and setOrders causes a render.
The URL should be absolute.
questions.explanation: Missing deps means the effect runs after every render; setting state re-renders; that runs the effect again. It's an infinite request loop that looks fine locally and turns into a denial of service on your own API in production. It needs [query]. The missing .catch is real but secondary.

questions.prompt: A table of 5,000 rows scrolls badly. Everything is already wrapped in useMemo. Now what?
options: Stop rendering 5,000 rows. Virtualise the list so only the visible window is in the DOM.
Memoise more aggressively — the row component and every callback.
Move the table's state into Redux.
Rewrite the table as class components.
questions.explanation: Memoisation stops unnecessary re-renders; it does nothing about 5,000 nodes the browser has to lay out and paint. Once the DOM itself is the bottleneck, the only real answer is to have less of it. Reaching for more useMemo here is the trap — it's the tool that worked last time.

questions.prompt: The app crashes because an API field typed as string came back null. TypeScript compiled it without complaint. Why?
options: A TypeScript bug — strictNullChecks should have caught it.
Types are erased at compile time. Nothing checked the actual response, so the declared type was a promise the server never agreed to.
The field should have been typed as any.
React should have caught it at the boundary.
questions.explanation: An interface describing an API response is documentation the compiler trusts absolutely and never verifies. Parse at the boundary — a schema validator that turns a bad response into a handled error rather than a crash three components deep. This is the single most common way TypeScript apps still fail at runtime.

questions.prompt: This counter increments to 1 and then stops.
options: count is captured once when the effect runs, so every tick computes 0 + 1. It needs the updater form: setCount(c => c + 1).
setInterval should be a recursive setTimeout.
The cleanup function is missing.
count should be held in a ref instead of state.
questions.explanation: The stale closure — the bug that makes people distrust hooks. The empty dependency array is right for the interval; it's the value read inside that's frozen. The updater form asks React for the current value instead of remembering one, which sidesteps the whole class of bug.

questions.prompt: A React team wraps nearly every value and callback in useMemo or useCallback. What is the best review response?
options: Keep it; memoization is always faster.
Remove React and use direct DOM APIs.
Replace every hook with global variables.
Memoize only where referential stability prevents measured work or satisfies a dependency contract; memoization itself has complexity and runtime cost.
questions.explanation: Memoization is a trade-off, not a default style. It pays when it avoids meaningful recalculation or downstream rendering, but indiscriminate use adds dependencies, allocations, and harder-to-read code without evidence of benefit.

questions.prompt: A list of draft submissions is rendered with key={index}. Delete the second row and the inputs below it show the wrong text. Why?
options: The rows should have been held in a ref rather than state.
Keys have to be strings, and index is a number.
After the delete the remaining rows shift up and inherit their neighbours' indexes, so React matches them to the wrong existing elements and the state sitting in those elements stays put.
The delete handler is mutating the array instead of replacing it.
questions.explanation: The key is how React decides which element is which between renders. Keyed by position, row three becomes row two and takes over row two's DOM node — along with whatever was typed into it. It only shows up in lists that reorder, delete, or hold their own state, which is why index keys survive so long before biting. A stable id from the data fixes it.

questions.prompt: The tag is added to the array — a console.log proves it — and the screen does not change. What is wrong?
options: push should be unshift, so the newest tag appears first.
The tag is pushed onto the same array and that array is handed straight back, so React compares it with itself, sees no change, and does not re-render. It needs a new array: setTags([...tags, tag]).
addTag should be wrapped in useCallback.
setTags should be called inside a useEffect.
questions.explanation: This is the bug where the data is right and the screen is wrong, and it sometimes half-fixes itself when something else causes a render — which is what makes it so confusing. React compares state by reference, so mutating in place is invisible to it. useCallback is the tempting answer because this is a callback and that is a hook; it changes nothing here.

questions.prompt: An empty submissions list renders a stray 0 above the empty-state message. The JSX is {submissions.length && <List items={submissions} />}. What is happening?
options: React cannot render an array of length zero.
&& returns the left-hand side when it is falsy, and 0 is falsy but also a perfectly renderable number — so React draws it.
The List component is returning 0 when it has nothing to show.
length should be length().
questions.explanation: The same guard works fine for undefined and null, because React renders nothing for those; 0 is the one falsy value it will happily paint on the screen. Use submissions.length > 0 && …, or a ternary. Blaming the child is the tempting move because that is where the 0 appears — the bug is in the guard, one line up.

questions.prompt: This runs whenever the selected form changes. Clicking quickly through the list sometimes leaves the wrong form on screen.
options: There is no cleanup, so a request that is still in flight when id changes still resolves and still sets state — and a slow earlier response can land after a newer one.
The dependency array should be empty.
fetch should be awaited inside an async function rather than chained with .then.
setForm should be wrapped in useCallback.
questions.explanation: Two requests are in the air and nothing promises they come back in order, so the slower first one wins and the UI shows a form nobody selected. The fix is a cleanup that ignores stale responses — a cancelled flag, or an AbortController on the request. Switching to async/await is a fair style preference that changes none of this: the earlier call still resolves.

questions.prompt: Editing works. But pick a different person from the list and the input still shows the previous name.
options: The input is uncontrolled and should use defaultValue instead of value.
onChange should be onInput to catch every keystroke.
The component should be wrapped in React.memo.
useState's argument is only the initial value — it is read on the first render and ignored on every one after, so a new user prop never reaches the input.
questions.explanation: Copying a prop into state creates a second source of truth, and state survives the re-render that the new prop arrives on. Either stop copying and let the parent own the edit, or force a fresh component per person with key={user.id} so useState runs again. defaultValue is the tempting one because it sounds like the mirror image of the problem — it makes the input uncontrolled, which throws away the state you were keeping.

questions.prompt: You are asked to add one field to a 700-line component nobody currently on the team wrote. First move?
options: Split it into smaller components first — the change will be much easier afterwards.
Copy the component, change the copy, and point the route at the new one.
Make the smallest change that works, and say in the pull request which parts of the file you did not understand.
Ask for the ticket to go to whoever knows that file best.
questions.explanation: The rewrite is tempting because the file genuinely is too big — and it turns a one-line change into a week of review nobody asked for, with regressions nobody can trace. Small change first. The honest note about what you did not follow is the part that pays: it points the reviewer at exactly where you are unsure, and it is how the refactor eventually gets agreed rather than smuggled in.
